title: WHAT IF YOU RODE A COMET 1.3 BILLION KM AWAY?

segments.line: You are sitting on a comet. Nobody on Earth knew it existed.
It is one point three billion kilometres from home.
And a telescope that was not even looking for comets just found you.
A streak. A smudge. Then a brand new world on the map.
This happened this autumn. ESA's Euclid made the catch.
So what if you rode that comet?
You'd be going the long way round.
Here are the rules.
You hold on to the comet. You do not let go.
You bring nothing. Space has plenty of room for nothing.
Cold is fine. You're wearing your usual hoodie.
The trip is long. One lap takes thousands of years.
So pack patience. Lots of patience.
First, though, meet your ride.
A comet is a dirty snowball. Ice, dust and rock.
It is left over from the birth of the Solar System.
That was about four point six billion years ago.
So you are sitting on something truly ancient.
Most comets come from the far edge: the Kuiper Belt or Oort Cloud.
Out there it is dark, still and very cold.
Then the Sun warms a comet, and it wakes up.
Ice turns to gas. Gas drags dust. A fuzzy cloud blooms around you.
Ice turns to gas. Gas drags dust. A fuzzy cloud blooms around you.
That cloud is the giveaway. It says this rock is active.
Hold that thought. The cloud is how they found you.
But who was looking? Nobody was.
Meet the one who was not looking.
Euclid is a European Space Agency telescope.
It launched in twenty twenty-three.
Its job is to stare at distant galaxies, slowly and deeply.
Long, steady pictures. Nothing fast. Nothing nearby.
Comets are fast and nearby. So, not its department.
On the sixteenth of September, Euclid starts taking pictures.
It keeps going until the twenty-fourth.
That is eight days of galaxies. And one passing stranger.
That stranger was you. Well, your comet.
It drifts across the shot like a fly across a window.
No one is watching live. The pictures just pile up.
Your comet could have slipped by unseen.
Until one person's software notices.
His name is Mikko Pöntinen, at the University of Helsinki.
He wrote a program to watch for small moving things.
It scans Euclid's pictures for streaks.
A streak means a fast mover smeared across several frames.
One day, it flags one.
He said, quote, I was excited to see my software flag a streak.
Now the hunt. Where does that streak go next?
He predicts its position. Then checks the other pictures.
It shows up again. And again.
Five separate image sets. Same object. Same path.
That's no glitch. Glitches do not move like that.
Then he zooms in on the dot.
And there it is. A fuzzy cloud around it.
Remember the cloud? Here is why it matters.
A plain rock would stay sharp. A fuzzy dot sheds dust and gas.
A plain rock would stay sharp. A fuzzy dot sheds dust and gas.
Fuzzy means active. Active means comet.
But is it new? Or has someone seen you before?
His team checks the catalogues of known comets and asteroids.
Row after row after row.
No match. You are not on any list.
That means you are brand new.
So Mikko reports it to the Minor Planet Center.
That's the group that keeps the official list.
The alert goes out. Telescopes on the ground can now take a look.
More eyes. More pictures. More proof.
On the eighth of October, it is official.
It is a comet. And it has a name.
Comet C slash twenty twenty-six S one. Euclid.
Euclid's very first new comet.
Now, where exactly are you sitting?
About one point three billion kilometres from Earth.
That is roughly between the orbits of Jupiter and Saturn.
Giants on both sides. Nobody around to wave to.
But you are not in the planets' flat lane.
The planets circle in one flat plane, like marbles on a table.
You are way above it. Straight up from the Sun.
Your path arches over the whole Solar System.
And one lap of that orbit takes thousands of years.
Whole civilisations would rise and fall. You would still be on lap one.
Whole civilisations would rise and fall. You would still be on lap one.
Honestly, bring a book. Maybe several libraries.
You drift. The Sun is a long way back.
Dust and gas stream out behind you.
Out here, you are small, cold, and completely alone.
Out here, you are small, cold, and completely alone.
Here is the wild part. This find was luck.
Euclid avoids the crowded band where comets and asteroids live.
That band throws off dust glare. Glare ruins deep pictures.
But you were not in that band. You were straight up.
Also, Euclid works in a step-and-stare style.
It usually visits each patch of sky only once.
So no second look on demand.
Yet it caught you in several images over those days.
One scientist at ESA called it a happy coincidence.
The right orbit. The right days. The right software.
Miss any one of them and you stay hidden for years.
So did Euclid just give humanity a ride-along?
Not quite. ESA has a mission called Comet Interceptor.
It will fly to a comet that is still far from the Sun.
Your comet turned out not to be the right target.
But ESA called this a real test case.
Spot a comet, alert the world, and coordinate fast.
Two teams practised that dance on you.
One telescope. One program. Five lucky pictures.
And a brand new comet, one point three billion kilometres away.
Remember the very first line? You are sitting on a comet.
Now you know how a telescope, a coder and luck found you.
Tomorrow: what if the Sun switched off for one hour?
Which comet would you ride? Tell me below.
